newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish settlements loom over Mideast peace summit.
newsitem.headline: Jewish settlements loom over Mideast peace summit.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday held crucial talks on the Middle East peace process, apparently deeply divided over Jewish settlements.
Mubarak and Netanyahu met in the Egyptian Red Sea resort as Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa held separate talks with his Israeli counterpart David Levy.

Moussa, asked by reporters before the meeting if the peace process was in crisis, said: "Absolutely." But he added the talks were intended to build a "positive atmosphere" to allow the peace process to resume.

"I don't want to say I'm pessimistic. I'm saying I'm hopeful that things will go in the right direction and the questions that have caused the frustration and the deterioration in the peace process will be dealt with," Moussa said at the airport.

Egypt made clear it would speak for the Palestinians, who refuse to resume peace talks with Israel until the Jewish state stops building settlements on Arab land occupied in the 1967 Middle War, including East Jerusalem.
But Netanyahu spokesman David Bar-Illan said before the meeting: "I don't know what you mean by freezing settlements. We cannot freeze building in places where people live.
"Obviously, if they are living in these places they grow, they get married and they have children. You cannot stop building in places where they are allowed to live." he told reporters.
Mubarak spoke by telephone from Sharm el-Sheikh to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Gaza. The two men also met in Cairo late on Monday to coordinate views.
Arafat was quoted by the Israeli daily Haaretz on Tuesday as saying he hoped the summit would revive peace talks stalled since March when Israel began a new settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

In the days before the Egypt summit, Israel announced it had approved plans to also build Arab housing in East Jerusalem. But Arafat said: "The problem isn't building for Palestinians, rather halting the settlements."
Asked if he would meet Netanyahu if building ceased, Arafat told reporters in Gaza: "The most important thing is what will happen today between President Mubarak and Mr Netanyahu."
Egyptian newspapers were sceptical the summit would produce progress and blamed Netanyahu for the crisis.
Moussa said settlements would be a summit issue but Netanyahu, who has vowed to expand Jewish settlement on occupied territory, had said the topic was not on his agenda.

"There are very important issues that we have to discuss. This is a discussion of the destinies of two people in a very small piece of land and that should be addressed, not details like whether there is going to be a housing project here or a housing project there," Bar-Illan said.
"To make that housing project an obstacle to peace is really to mock the peace process," he told reporters.
In remarks to Haaretz, Arafat warned of a "disaster" unless there was progress in peacemaking. Moussa said he hoped Netanyahu would change his mind about the settlement.
The U.S. ambassador to Israel said he did not expect breakthroughs at the Egypt meeting but Israel's Levy said he hoped the meeting would help break the impasse.

"We are making a joint effort to solve matters. I hope we will succeed. Of course it doesn't depend on Israel alone but on both sides. It is an important meeting and I hope the result also will be important," Levy said on arrival in Egypt.
